en: In the *Sūtra on the Buddha’s Teaching of the Visualization of Maitreya Bodhisattva’s Rebirth in Tuṣita Heaven*, it is described that the Dharma of Great Compassion extracts suffering and bestows happiness.
Great Benevolence (*maitrī*) takes the wholesome root of non-aversion as its essence; Great Compassion (*karuṇā*) takes the absence of both aversion and delusion as its nature.
Each of these has three aspects. First is the object consisting of sentient beings (*sattvālambana*), so called because it takes conventionally designated sentient beings as its object.

Second is the condition of dharmas (*dharmālambana*): because one does not perceive sentient beings, there are only dharmas. Third is the unconditioned (*anālambana*): even the characteristics of dharmas are absent, for there is only ultimate truth (*tattva*).

Alternatively, "conditioned by sentient beings" means arising by taking sentient beings as its object; "conditioned by dharmas" means arising by taking the twelvefold teaching (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*) as its object;
"unconditioned" means arising by taking suchness (*tathatā*) as its object, because there is no objective referent. Because Maitreya compassionately guides all things, he thus expounds [this].
Regarding the Dharma of Compassion, Tanwuchen stated: "Within these precious trees, there are also golden pheasants, precious phoenixes, white sparrows, and red sparrows;
these are omitted from the description for brevity. One should verify this further."
Regarding the statement that "each wall is fourteen yojanas thick," the commentary says:
this refers to the fourth broad wall. "Wall" (yuan) here means a garden enclosure. It is sixty-two yojanas high.

It is revealed that those born there surpass and shatter the sixty-two views. "A thickness of fourteen *yojanas*" signifies the mastery and destruction of the fourteen points of indeterminacy (*avyākṛta*).
Master Ying says: "The Sanskrit term is *yojana*; here it is translated as 'a combined measure' (*he*).

One should calculate that the breadth is exactly this much; it is equivalent to a *li* (Chinese mile) in this region. Another interpretation is that it refers to a standard measure (*liang*). From [here]...
The ancient sage-kings traveled one day’s journey; although the commentaries explain this differently, we shall now follow the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*:
five hundred bows (*dhanus*) constitute one *krośa*, and eight *krośas* constitute one *yojana*. What is currently called a *yōjūn* (yojana) is a corruption and abbreviation of this term.
This signifies that those born in the heavens all transcend the eight false conceptions, which are [included within] the sixty-two views and so forth.

Because of their fundamental nature, among these four adornments, the first two constitute progressive advancement, both ultimately converging upon the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*); this is because there are distinctions between the initial generation of the resolve (*cittotpāda*) and the realization of the fruit.
The next one destroys anger and ignorance to rescue the classes of sentient beings; the final one eternally distances one from the heterodox views of non-Buddhists.

Due to these superior functions, they are emphasized and further elucidated. "Wall" (*yuan*) refers to the surrounding enclosure. The *Shiming* (Explanations of Names) states: [the wall is so called because it encloses and protects].
A fence or enclosure (*yuan*) is that which people rely upon for obstruction, serving as a defensive protection; a wall (*qiang*) is a barrier, used for self-concealment.
As for those five hundred billion [beings] who surround this enclosure:
The commentary states: Third, there are three aspects of the dragon king’s protection. First, the dragon’s protection; second, the raining of jewel-trees;
and third, the trees preaching the Dharma. This is the first. The Dharma King universally transforms all beings, and celestial deities provide guard and vigilance for fear of external invasion.
Regarding the "five hundred billion": this manifests that internally he possesses the five powers, such that the four māras cannot subdue him; externally...
There is a dragon king whom non-humans cannot oppress or harm. Internally, he upholds the five precepts, so that no evils may invade him;
externally, he is surrounded by a retinue of dragons, such that calamities are extinguished on their own. Question: Is this dragon king a transformation-body or a real being?

Answer: He is a transformation-dragon. Question: Are there also real dragon kings in the celestial palaces? Answer: There are indeed, but they are only transformation-dragon kings who possess no poisonous malice.
Therefore, this manifestation of adornments is what is displayed through the power of Maitreya’s great compassionate vows.
As for each of the dragon kings [up to] adorning the top of the wall:
The commentary states: This is the tree that rains jewels. Because the seven riches arise from the five faculties, the dragon king is moved to rain down these trees.

Those who adorn themselves with the seven noble riches are: faith, ethical discipline, learning, renunciation, wisdom, shame, and remorse. These are explained in detail in the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*.
"Spontaneously there is wind... up to the various pāramitās. The commentary states:
"This subsequent section describes the tree preaching the Dharma. The wind is a metaphor for great compassion, which spontaneously blows upon and strikes both the ultimate and conventional truths."
The wise tree touches upon these matters, expounding such teachings as these: namely, that all things subject to outflows (*āsrava*) have a nature of oppression and are grasped as suffering;

that the essence of phenomena (*dharma*) is entirely non-existent and thus called "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*); and that conditioned things (*saṃskṛta*) arise and cease, undergoing flux, birth, and destruction.
There is no collective self-essence, nor a permanent, unitary, and real self. Because it enables all practitioners to transcend and reach the other shore, it is called a *pāramitā*.
Although the above has been explained analytically, it should now be explained synthetically: this arises from the palace following the fulfillment of vows.
It was adorned with gardens of the seven treasures, where flowers bloomed in response to light. It was further embellished with ten billion fruits, and moreover, crystal emitted radiant colors.
From these [fruits], the sounds of compassion issued forth in a winding melody.

With jewels as its primary feature, it was named the Hall of Dharma Creation. To speak of it in terms of its actual construction, it served as the inner courtyard. Its textual description also has three parts; first:
The Great Deity first made a vow; next, the fruits of that vow were fulfilled; finally, the various devas, beholding this excellence, vowed to be reborn there.
This section consists of two parts: first, the ritual protocol, and second, the making of the vow. This is the former.
*Laudovaditi* (牢度跋提) means "Lord of Evil" (*āśubhādhipati*), as he is the lord who governs evil. He is a spirit (*bhūta*) similar to the yakṣa-devas in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

Its reality is hidden and unfathomable; it is called "Spirit" (*śen*). Among spirits, that which is most supreme is called "Great. Universally relying upon its majestic power, one pays homage throughout the ten directions.
Desiring to understand this vastness, one gives rise to great vows. Although one knows that both ordinary beings and sages alike respond within the Inner Court, [one must still strive].
Only then is the power of a bodhisattva fully realized; its increase is due to the manifestation of the noble ones. Regarding the "one great divine power":

it signifies that untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) is capable of giving rise to a wondrous land. The *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states: "It is produced by supramundane roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) and possesses divine efficacy like a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*).
Furthermore, it is also induced by the preparatory wisdom (*prayoga-jñāna*) of ordinary beings who have resolved upon bodhicitta.
"If by my merit [the jewel] emerges spontaneously. The commentary states:
This is the subsequent vow. It proclaims the sublime meaning; it is named the Hall of Good Dharma (*Saddharmasabhā*) to signify profound respect.

A jewel emerged from his forehead. The palatial buildings of the inner court were as described in his own account below. Because the Dharma Hall was most sublime, it was designated at the head of his vows.
Having thus made his vow (up to the point where it says) "shining through both inside and out":

The commentary states: There are five ways in which the fruits of the second vow were fulfilled: first, the construction of palaces; second, the construction of gardens; third, the construction of seats;

fourth, the construction of pillars; and fifth, the celestial palaces and goddesses having identical precious colors. Furthermore, there are eight types of palaces in the first category. First, the construction of palaces.
1. The two railings; 2. The daughters of the devas; 3. Flowers arising from the hands; 4. Radiance; 5. Musical instruments;
6. Rising to dance; 7. Preaching the Dharma. Regarding the first [the railings], there are two parts: first, the emergence of the jewels, and second, the construction of the palace.
This is the former. The lapis lazuli is emerald-green and the crystal is crimson. Taking these green and red as the primary path for the jewels upon the forehead, all other colors follow suit.
Everything is complete. Or rather, these two treasures possess every variety of color in full. "Purple" (*zǐ*) refers to the color purple. Regarding "gān" (*jiàn*):
the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it is silk of a deep blue that reflects a reddish hue; "gān" means to contain. It is blue while containing red.
The "gān" used here differs slightly from that definition, being like a purple-blue. As for the "beads," they are *vaidūrya* (lapis lazuli) and *sphatika* (crystal).
The color of the pear is like the light of a purple-blue *maṇi* jewel, luminous within and without; thus it is transparent from both sides.
This signifies that Maitreya has heard the gates of ten billion *dhāraṇīs*, wherein no signless state remains unmanifested and no obstruction remains unpurified.
Regarding the phrase "this Maṇi-light... to the subtle and wondrous jewel palace," the commentary states:

"This refers to the construction of the palace hereafter. As for the "forty-nine tiers," it signifies that because the observance of the precepts is firm and secure, the palace consequently becomes layered and dense.

This symbolizes that Maitreya has already transcended the forty mental states, such as the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*), as well as the nine stages beginning with the Stage of Extreme Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
He dwells in the Cloud of Dharma (Dharmameghā). Thus, his palace has forty-nine tiers, corresponding to the forty-nine stages of his cultivated practice.
Each and every railing, down to those elements that together constitute the whole, is thus formed.
The commentary states: "The second [feature] is the construction of the balustrade (vedikā). The dhāraṇīs are like a balustrade;

this is because Maitreya presides over ten billion dhāraṇīs. As for the external manifestation of ten trillion *maṇi* jewels, there are variations in their quantity, yet there is no contradiction between the preceding and following descriptions."
Regarding the passage from "between the various railings" to "five hundred *koṭi* of celestial maidens," the Commentary states:
The third is the emanated son of heaven (*devaputra*). The celestial maiden is skillful means (*upāya*), for she sustains all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).

The son is wisdom (*prajñā*), for he plants the seeds of the roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*). These two are distinct, as explained in detail in the *Maitreya-paripṛcchā-śāstra*. This refers to the planting of the seeds of virtue.
Although they are numerous, they must necessarily arise from the wisdom of nine grades; hence it is said there are "nine hundred million.
Although the skillful means are manifold, they rely on the power of the five faculties, such as faith, to traverse a realm of ten billion worlds; hence it is said there are "five hundred billion."
Regarding the passage from "each and every son of heaven" to "seven-jeweled flowers," the Commentary states:

The fourth hand produces lotus flowers. Although the functions of *prajñā* (wisdom) are immeasurable, they all arise from the seven treasures of the noble ones (*saptadhanas*), for these contain the perfect fruit.
Thus, externally, they manifest billions of seven-jeweled flowers; in principle, this is indeed the skillful means (*upāya*).
It contains the fruits of the Way; however, because it merely anticipates the function of *prajñā*, it is not mentioned.
[The passage from] "not being struck but sounding of itself" [is as follows].
The commentary states: "The sixth refers to the musical instruments of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (*Nirmāṇarati*).

By the power of wisdom, their eloquence is unimpeded, and they are able to give rise to hearts of joy in sentient beings; therefore, they are called 'instruments of music. Since Maitreya already dwells in the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), he is entirely without effort regarding all illnesses and medicines;
hence it is said that 'they sound without being struck.'"
Regarding the passage from "When this sound issues forth" to "those who compete by rising to sing and dance," the commentary states:
"The seventh is the rising for dance. Once the musical sounds have moved, the women rise and dance; this immediately symbolizes eloquence."
The responsive chanting is a skillful means, and it also manifests physical transformations to benefit sentient beings.
As for the phrase "at that time, those who [hear] the sound of the songs [and develop] the mind for the unsurpassed Way," the commentary states:
this is the eighth teaching of the Dharma. Although it takes the form of song, it does not rely on the play of birth and death; rather, it expounds [the truth].

The ten wholesome actions and the four great vows demonstrate that Maitreya’s benefit extends not only to physical deeds (*kāyakarman*), but also to verbal deeds (*vākkarman*) through his transformative teachings.
The ten wholesome actions are the cause for rebirth in the heavens; the four great vows are the cause for attaining the Way.
What are these four? The *Sūtra of the Seven Buddhas* states: First, to nurture and protect all sentient beings, like a boat that ferries people across.
1. To be free from weariness. 2. To encompass all things within two joints, like the great void. 3.
To wish that my own body may be like a medicinal tree, such that whoever hears [its name] shall have all their ailments and sufferings completely removed. 4.

To wish that when I attain Buddhahood in the future, the sentient beings I deliver shall be as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River. These constitute the Bodhisattva’s mind of salvation and the provisions for enlightenment (*bodhi-sambhāra*).
The treatise says: "If there are sentient beings who have not yet been delivered, I shall deliver them; those who are not yet liberated, I shall liberate;
those who have not yet found rest, I shall cause to find rest; those who have not yet attained nirvana, I shall lead to nirvana.

Since the sūtras and treatises are truly vast and the vows are manifold, it is not contradictory to discuss even a single meaning from among them. Therefore, when the various devas heard this, they gave rise to the Great [Vow].
The vehicle of the mind. One generates the Mahāyāna mind through seven causes and conditions. As stated in the *Dharmamudrā-sūtra*:
"There are seven kinds of causes for generating the bodhicitta: first, the exhortation of all Buddhas; second, seeing that the Dharma is about to perish;
third, giving rise to great compassion for all sentient beings; fourth, the instruction of Bodhisattvas; fifth, because of the practice of giving."
Sixth, learning from others; seventh, hearing the description of the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics.
Among these, the first three types of resolve can protect the true Dharma and swiftly achieve unsurpassed enlightenment. The remaining four types of resolve do not belong to true bodhisattvas;
they cannot protect and uphold the true Dharma held by the Buddhas, nor can they swiftly achieve unsurpassed enlightenment. This present resolve [is of the former kind].
Since these arise from the teaching of Maitreya Bodhisattva, they are not [ultimately] real.

These eight adornments above are realized through the Eightfold Noble Path of holy practice and the experience of the bliss of the eight liberations; they are the results sequentially induced by those who uphold the eight precepts.

All the practices of both the noble and the ordinary are integrated through the assistance of right wisdom and so forth. Thus, with wisdom as the precursor, they are arranged and arrayed, whereby they are able to—
Thus it is brought about. Were it not so, for what reason would there be such a sublime place? Although the above has been explained analytically, it should now be interpreted as a whole.
Indeed, the exquisite palace is adorned with mani-jewel railings; celestial red lotuses manifest, their radiance containing the joy of purity.
Thereupon, the Jewel Wisdom resounds of its own accord, dancing repeatedly upon clouds borne by wheels. Pure songs emerge from the sages, and they hear the Dharma.
"By focusing the mind upon these sounds, such inconceivable power of aspiration is attained;
thus, this adornment is achieved. Regarding the passage from "At that time, within the various gardens... to "...the lapis lazuli conduits," the commentary states:
The second section, the construction of the gardens, has two parts: first, the analysis of the seven matters of adornment; second, the conclusion regarding the birth therein. First:
There are seven [types of waterways], and this is the first of the eight channels of form (*rūpa*). As for the "eight forms," they are blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, purple, azure, and green.
These symbolize that Maitreya has already achieved the mastery of the eight kinds of discipline (*saṃvara*), as he necessarily relies upon the channel of ethical conduct (*śīla*).
According to one interpretation, the channels are made of eight-colored lapis lazuli, and thus they are called "eight-colored"; this interpretation is also plausible.
Regarding the statement that each individual channel (culminating in) is used to form a synthesis, the commentary says:
"The second [level] is formed by the synthesis of precious jewels. These various jewels metaphorically represent the hundred practices (*śata-karman*).

Since the hundred practices are synthesized into the *saṃvara* (restraint), and since these hundred practices necessarily arise from the five faculties such as faith (*pañcendriya*), it is said to be 'five hundred million'."
Regarding the statement that "each channel contains water of eight flavors," the commentary says:
this refers to the third matter of the eight flavors; that is, because each of the aforementioned eight colors possesses all eight flavors. Some say: [this is so].
Regarding the water of eight qualities: it is called "eightfold" because its taste is delightful and because it represents the Eightfold Noble Path.
As for the water surging upward like flowing jewel-flowers: [it reaches] as far as... (as above).
The commentary states: "The fourth [section] describes the production of the four flowers. As for the four flowers, they are blue, yellow, red, and white.
These are the eight waters of the channels that flow around the rainbow bridge, surging with waves; their colors manifest as the four flowers, which reflect the crimson gate and scatter their hues.
Furthermore, the water of eight colors emerges from the flowers, and the flowers of four colors arise from the water; the colors of the water and the flowers intermingle."
"Reflecting like flowing jewel-flowers: this symbolizes the Eightfold Noble Path, which shall manifest the fruits of the four virtues, such as permanence.
Regarding each flower [up to] the adorned physical marks:"
The commentary states: Fifth is the goddess Huasheng (Flower-Born). Regarding the fruits such as "constancy" and so forth, there must necessarily be skillful means (*upāya*).

The root of these skillful means is precisely the observance of the precepts (*śīla*). This signifies that by observing the sevenfold precepts, one guards against the evils of the three periods of time and thereby receives the three kinds of goodness.
Regarding the twenty-four fruits of retribution, the phrase "naturally [filling] the hands until they are spontaneously full" is explained as follows:
the sixth hand produces jeweled vessels; the hand symbolizes the teaching (*śāsana*). The *Tattvasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* states: "The hand of the True Dharma Teaching."

Therefore, this represents the sentient beings of the great trichiliocosm who hear and receive the True Dharma, giving rise to faith, diligence, and so forth, such that the five faculties proceed together with the desire for wholesome dharmas;
hence it is said there are "five hundred billion," which refers to those who have first resolved their minds [for enlightenment] and come according to their respective vehicles.
Because they suddenly hope for the fruit of the Way, it is said that "the nectar is full.
Regarding the phrase "shouldering the six *pāramitās* on the left shoulder," the commentary states:
the seventh goddess emerges from the water. All the goddesses wear necklaces (*hāra*) on their left sides and carry [their offerings] on their right.
Musical instruments emerge from the water of form, abiding in the sky like auspicious clouds. With their mouths they praise the Bodhisattva’s practice of the six perfections.
This represents the left attendant of Maitreya, who possesses the mark of excellence and, on the right, eloquence;
emerging from the void like clouds containing rain, they shower the rain of the True Dharma to benefit sentient beings. In brief, it is said that all who uphold the sevenfold precepts and...
She has cultivated the seven noble riches and practiced the seven factors of enlightenment, thereby eliminating that which is summoned by the seven latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Such a celestial maiden, Oṣadhī, may not actually be a woman; she may have been conjured through the collective transformation of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas to adorn the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), or she may have appeared as a result of a woman’s past maintenance of pure precepts and diligence, free from transgression. She cannot be grasped by an ordinary mind.
Regarding what is measured:
if there are those who are reborn [in that realm] and are attended by celestial maidens, it is stated:
"In the second [life], they obtain rebirth there. This indicates that sentient beings born in that heaven will attain Maitreya.
This refers to skillful means for conversion and guidance.
There are also [seats] made of the seven treasures, reaching a height of four *yojanas*.
The commentary states: "The adornment of the third seat has two parts: first, the dimensions of the seat’s height and breadth; second, the jewel adornment of the seat."
This is the first [section]. What are the seven treasures? As stated in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* (The Sutra Praising the Pure Land):
first, gold; second, silver; third, vaidūrya; fourth, sphaṭika; fifth, red pearl; sixth, aśmagarbha;
seventh, musāragalva. The commentary explains: as for the two treasures of gold and silver, since they exist in this land, all teachings...
[The character] "cun" (to exist/preserve). To preserve this name [of the place]. Paramārtha says: *vairāga* in the Sanskrit sound;
this means "yellow jewel," which is gold. *Candragana* in the Sanskrit sound; this means "white jewel," which is silver.
*Vaiḍūrya* is the correct Sanskrit form. *Vaiḷūrya* is a corruption. The *Paramārtha’s Commentary on the Treatise* (Liang-lun-chao) says: "Vaiḍūrya..."
*Vaiḍūrya* is a blue-colored jewel; it cannot be destroyed by fire, and only spirits (*devayoni*) possessing supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) can break it to fashion it into vessels.
It may also be the egg of the *garuḍa*. *Sphaṭika* is a yellowish-green jewel.
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* calls it the *karketanaka* jewel, while the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that after a thousand years, ice [transforms into it].
It transforms into crystal beads. Regarding "red pearls," the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:
they are called red pearls because they are produced by red insects, or because the substance of the bead itself is red. Paramārtha says: they are, in fact, priceless precious jewels.
*Aśmagarbha* means agate; Paramārtha says it is a red-colored gem, which contradicts the *Nirabhilāpyadharmatāsiddhi-śāstra*.
That treatise states that it is [a type of] *indranīla* (sapphire) and so forth. *Musāragalva* was formerly called "carriage-shell" (*chequ*);
Paramārtha says it is a deep blue gem. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Gold is found within mountain rocks, sand, and red copper."
Pearls are produced from the bellies of fish and from within bamboo. Snake-brain and dragon-pearls are produced from dragon-camphor (*nāgakesara*).

Coral is produced from the sea; it is a stone that has transformed into crystal beads. The *Daye lun* (Treatise on the Great Matter) states: "The seven treasures are all comprised within the category of stone. Nevertheless, as for the seven treasures...
Respected according to the region, the sūtras and śāstras differ; one should not harbor doubts about this. Question:
Why is this seat of the seven treasures called a "lion seat" (*siṃhāsana*)? Answer: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that the Buddha is the lion among men;

therefore, wherever the Buddha sits—whether on a couch or upon the ground—it is all termed a "lion seat. A detailed explanation is found in the *Dṛṣṭānta-saṃgraha-sūtra*, which says: "Five hundred lions heard..."
The Buddha appeared in the world and transformed all sentient beings, causing them all to be reborn as devas or humans.
When birds and beasts were exhausted, he harbored poison in his heart and intended to go and harm the Buddha. The Buddha immediately manifested a most exquisite seat and sat upon the head of a lion.
When the multitude saw this, it was called the "Lion Seat. By obtaining this seat, one attains that wisdom.
Regarding the discourse on the pure dharma-realm, it inherently contains four virtues.
The seat of the transformation body is four yojanas high and is adorned with Jāmbūnada gold.
The commentary states: "Regarding this lion throne, there are nine kinds of adornments; this is the adornment of precious gold.

Because Maitreya’s three karmas proceed in accordance with wisdom and thus transcend the adornments of ordinary beings and those of the Lesser Vehicle, it is called the 'Golden Lion Throne' in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*."
Regarding the four lotus flowers that grow at the four corners of the seat, the Commentary states:
"This is the second adornment of flowers. Because of the four immeasurables—compassion, mercy, joy, and equanimity—within, four flowers are manifested externally."
Regarding the second [lotus], "that which is composed of a hundred jewels," the commentary states:

this refers to the adornment of the three hundred jewels. Because one practices the ten paths of wholesome action—whether by performing them oneself, teaching others to do so, or praising and rejoicing in them—whether in small measure, great measure, or in full;
whether for a short time, a long time, or for the duration of one's life; there are ten instances for each.

It is named "The Hundred Practices. Internally it is cultivated through internal practices; externally it is composed of a hundred jewels. This is why the number "hundred" is frequently mentioned throughout the sutra.
As for each jewel emitting ten billion rays of light:

The commentary states: "The fourth is the Adornment of Radiance. Because the wisdom produced by a hundredfold practices emits light, and because insight destroys the darkness of ignorance, its radiance is subtle and wondrous...
[extending to] the adornment of the precious canopy."

The commentary states: "The fifth is the Adornment of the Precious Canopy. Because one simultaneously cultivates the aids to practice, such as faith, along with the hundred [primary] practices, it is called 'five hundred billion.
Because the various practices assist one another, it is called 'variegated flowers' (Saṃpuṣpita)."
Regarding the phrase "at that time, the ten directions (extending to... are made into jeweled bells," the commentary states:

this is the sixth adornment of Brahma-jewels. Internally, one cultivates the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*); externally, there are great Brahma-bells suspended. Great beings revere this.

This symbolizes that Maitreya, having passed through hundreds of thousands of kalpas since attaining equal enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), dwells in his final position and cultivates [these qualities].
The practice of the ten stages results in the perfection of eloquence.
Regarding the passage from "at that time, the minor Brahmā king" up to "pervading the canopy above," the commentary states:
this refers to the seventh [stage], the Adornment of the Brahmā Net. This is because internally one cultivates *dhāraṇī*, and externally one attains the minor Brahmā as a net.
In brief, as one is about to expound the definitive teaching, one first prepares the lion throne to demonstrate its magnificent and exquisite adornment;
for it is polished with the finest essence, the golden path radiates the light of a hundred jewels,
and pearl canopies hang like a thousand Brahma-nets, thus it is said that they cover it completely above.
Regarding the passage from "At that time, hundreds of thousands... up to "...who spread cloth upon the seat," the commentary states:

This eighth section, "The Adornment of the Flower-Spread Seat," signifies that because Maitreya’s *prajñā* and *upāya* have already reached fulfillment, he will certainly attain the fruit of the unsurpassed path.
Regarding these various lotus flowers (up to) those standing in attendance within the canopy, the commentary states:
"The ninth heavenly maiden attending the canopy represents Maitreya’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), the hand that expounds the True Dharma, who transforms and guides ten billion beings.
She stands in the center, representing the *nirvāṇa-dhātu*. With these nine adornments, added to the previous measurements of the seat, there are ten."

This magnificence is entirely brought about by ordinary beings who eliminate the ten unwholesome paths of action and cultivate the ten wholesome ones, or by Bodhisattvas who likewise cultivate the ten inexhaustible precepts;
it is that which these precepts have summoned forth.
At that time, there were precious pillars at each of the four corners of the palace.

The commentary states: "The fourth section, 'The Pillars,' has four parts: first, the precious pillars supporting the palace; second, the interlaced *maṇi* jewel ornaments; third, the musical sounds within the galleries;

and fourth, the proclamation of the Dharma through those musical sounds. This is the first. Tánshí interpreted this as referring to the four pillars supporting the forty-nine tiers of the Dharma Hall.
Furthermore, it may also refer to the four precious pillars adorning the four corners outside the hall.
The implements of adornment. First, following the text of the sūtra:
regarding each jeweled pillar [up to] the various pāramitās, the commentary states:
□□□□. As for *brahmanī*, it means *viśuddha-maṇi* (pure maṇi), or the wish-fulfilling gem of the Great Brahmā King.
With pearl pillars of various adornments,
such celestial palaces likewise possess the same jewel-colored radiance.
The commentary states: The fifth [group] consists of the celestial maidens, all of whom possess jewel-like complexions.
This is intended to manifest the various adornments of the inner court, so as to cause sentient beings to enter together into the Buddha’s wisdom.
Regarding the passage from "At that time, throughout the ten directions" up to "the Tuṣita Heaven Palace," the commentary states:
Third, the various devas behold the excellence [of Maitreya] and make vows to be reborn there. Once reborn, they all subsequently make vows;
yet there are also those who make vows even before being reborn. To speak of them collectively, it is because of the precious lotus flower seats and the heavens.
Young attendants guard the curtains; pearl pillars support the palace, interlaced with *maṇi* jewels. As pure music resounds with a clanging clarity, the six perfections form its harmonious rhythm.
The precious light is brilliant and pure, reflecting the colors of all the devas.

Beholding this compassionate splendor and supreme adornment, there is none who does not dwell upon it with reverence, take refuge, and vow to be born in Tuṣita. This above describes the second great deity.
Once the construction of the inner court was completed, there were five great deities in the Tuṣita Heaven palace. As it is stated:
"The third [section] distinguishes the five great deities; regarding the various adornments of the outer and inner palaces, there are two parts. First..."

This is the initial section of the general heading, followed by the specific exposition. Because Bodhisattvas and others internally cultivate the five aggregates (*skandha*), their wondrous functions are boundless;

externally, they manifest five deities whose majestic power is peerless. Question: If it is said that there are deities in the heavens, does it follow that other realms of existence (*gati*) exist within the heavens?
Answer: Heavenly oxen and heavenly horses are themselves animals, ghosts, and so forth. As for Śakra...

Regarding the dwelling places: now, as there is the path of ghosts and spirits within the celestial palaces created by deities, and since there are already ghosts and animals, there must likewise be humans and hells.
Just as it is with the heavens, so it should be for the others; therefore, each must cultivate their respective realms accordingly. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
In the Dharma of human life, there are two types of devas who provide protection: the first is named *Tongming* (Same Name), and the second is named *Tongsheng* (Same Birth).

These devas can see humans, but humans cannot see these devas; thus, there are devas among humanity. Furthermore, it is said that there are devas of the night, devas of the water, and devas of the earth.
Since "deva" refers to a general category, this principle applies to all realms of existence, which then constitute the five destinies (*pañca-gati*). Each of these destinies has its own...
Five. There are twenty-five paths in five groups of five; such is the nature of provisional categories.
Regarding the first great deity (up to) "that which accords with the inclinations of sentient beings," the commentary states:
the second [section] specifically reveals five [deities]; this is the first deity. Internally upholding the aggregate of ethical discipline, one attains exalted status.
Like a precious banner, lofty and manifest, the seven branches of the precepts rain down the seven treasures.
Through the observance of these precepts, each according to the inclinations of people's hearts, they evoke the sound of music that accords with the minds of all beings.
Regarding the second great deity (up to) "acting as the guide":

the commentary states that this refers to the fruition of the aggregate of meditative concentration (*samādhi-skandha*). Internally, one cultivates the aggregate of emptiness; externally, one manifests the virtue of flowers.

Because the water of concentration is utterly pure, wondrous flowers emerge. By giving rise to the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), one extends protection over the four modes of birth; thus, a rain of various flowers falls, transforming them into [the state of] Buddhahood.
The flower-canopy and immeasurable multitudes of practices assist in adorning meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). One hundred thousand banners arise as a guide.
As for the third great deity [who] circles the palace seven times:

The commentary states: This is the fruition of the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*). Internally possessing the aggregate of wisdom, he preaches the Dharma to benefit sentient beings and destroys the stench of ignorance.
Externally, he manifests as a great deity named Gandharva (Fragrant Sound). His fragrance reaches this shore [of the world] to the extent of six *li*.

Its value is equivalent to that of the Sahā world; his wisdom may be measured as being like the ocean. Because the fragrance of this shore can eliminate the seven outflows (*āsrava*), he circumambulates seven times.

Next, the seven outflows (*āsrava*) are: the outflow of views, the outflow of mindfulness, the outflow of craving, the outflow of cultivation, the outflow of the faculties, the outflow of evil, and the outflow of intimacy; these are explained in detail in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Fourth, the Great Deity who [provides] the Sound that Assists Bodhi.
The commentary states: This is the fruit of the aggregate of liberation (*vimukti-skandha*). Internally, it is filled with the aggregate of liberation;

externally, it manifests a great deity named "Joyful Bliss" (*pramuditānanda*), who is far removed from sorrow and suffering and has attained the joy of supreme resolve (*adhimukti*). Since the mind is thus determined, the practice can be perfected;
therefore, wish-fulfilling jewels (*cintāmaṇi*) rain down. With the mind constantly determined, one abides in *tathatā* (suchness), and externally, the deity dwells there.
Regarding the banners and streamers: having already spoken of the Three Refuges, they further speak of the Five Precepts and various wholesome dharmas.

"Benefiting" (rāo-yi) means the sense of profit and happiness; "exhorting" (quan) means the sense of praise and encouragement; "assisting" (zhu) means the sense of providing resources, benefit, and mutual support. "Sound" (yin) refers to vocal sound; "one who" (zhe) refers to the practitioner.
This collectively reveals the divine jewel, which expounds the profit and happiness of the Three Refuges, the Five Precepts, and so forth, and exhorts [others].
Regarding those practitioners who aspire to seek great Bodhi, it is indicated that they dwell among ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*);
however, I dare not definitively determine this. It is simply that the Great Sage manifests his body according to the diverse dispositions of sentient beings, and thus their perceptions differ.
Since their visions are not the same, how could they be born in the same place? Based on this reasoning, there is no cause for wonder. According to one interpretation, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*...
This refers to the place where they were nurtured; therefore, there is no contradiction. For parents do not merely give birth, but also provide nourishment.
Otherwise, how could the *Xianyu jing* state: "When the king heard this, his heart was distressed and he became fearful, fearing that [the child] would seize his kingdom"?

He waited until [the child] was no longer small before intending to remove him. Once the palace attendants learned of this, they secretly informed his parents, who privately sent him to his maternal uncle’s household to avoid danger and pursue his studies.
Daoshi said: "The *Xiányújīng* (Sūtra on the Wise and the Foolish) indicates the place of birth; the *Shàngshēngjīng* (Sūtra on the Birth in the Heavens) points to the place of upbringing."
The uncle’s name was Parāli. Thus, although there are three interpretations, the second is superior. This is because the first contradicts Maitreya’s initial teaching;
it conflicts with various passages and lacks a coherent interpretation of their intended meaning.
Furthermore, while the latter [interpretation] accords with two sūtras, it still contradicts the *Avataṃsaka*.
"He sits in the full lotus posture as if entering the meditative absorption of cessation.
The commentary states: "This is the third aspect of entering cessation. 'Jie' (結) means to bind together; 'jia' (跏) means to double over.

Śākyamuni sat with his right side toward the ground and his hand as a pillow to enter *nirvāṇa*, signifying that his conditions for transformation were exhausted. This reveals that Maitreya Buddha’s benefit and joy for sentient beings have not yet ended."

In the end, one shall attain the wisdom of fruition (*phala-jñāna*), for only then will all phenomena be exhausted; thus, the two aspects differ, signifying the distinction between the ultimate and the non-ultimate.

Although it resembles entry into *nirvāṇa*, in reality there is no perfect extinction, as one is about to be reborn in the higher realms, just as when entering the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
Regarding "the body is purple-gold in color... reaching the Tuṣita Heaven," the commentary states:
this describes the fourth mark of being born last. That the body is purple-gold in color signifies that his birth shall be the most preeminent.
That he is like hundreds of thousands of suns signifies that he can shatter the delusion of permanence held by sentient beings.
Regarding "its bodily relics (up to) being unmoving and unshaking," the commentary states:
"The fifth is the form of the relic (*śarīra*). *Śarīra* means grain; *dhātu* means substance."

The Buddha’s body is the size of a grain of rice; thus it is given this name. Śākyamuni Tathāgata’s division of his relics into fragments symbolizes the manifestation of his divided bodies throughout the ten directions to guide and benefit many.
Maitreya’s whole body symbolizes his residence in Tuṣita Heaven, where he carries out the transformative work of a single Buddha.
Just as cast gold does not waver, this symbolizes that the Buddha’s Dharma-body is fundamentally without birth or extinction.

Regarding the incident of its movement: furthermore, it was observed that its bulk remained as usual, its length did not change, it could not be stretched even when struck with a hammer, and its color resembled that of a golden statue;
therefore, it was presumed to be cast gold.
Regarding the phrase "within the circular halo of the body, the meaning of the letter *zhi* (*jihvā*) is radiant," the commentary states:
This is the sixth miraculous manifestation of the circular halo, namely the *brahmasvara-samādhi*.

"Samādhi" is translated here as "equal holding" (*samādhāraṇa*); "samāya" is a corruption. It is a sublime concentration within the Mahāyāna, wherein both the letter *zhi* and its meaning are vividly manifest.
"Brightly manifest" (*bingran*) is another name for "radiant splendor. This meaning indicates that within the circular halo there are both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
The meaning of the characters is radiant, and the stūpa is clearly manifest. Because the meaning becomes evident upon beholding the text, the meaning is said to be "manifest" (*xian*).
Otherwise, how could light be able to manifest meaning? Although [the Buddha] has entered extinction, his meditative concentration and wisdom remain perfected.
Minghuan: *Śūraṅgama* means "Valiant Progress" (*jianxing*).
Because it is attained only by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage, according to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, there are five names for it: first, *Śūraṅgama*; second, *Prajñāpāramitā*;
third, *Vajra*; fourth, *Siṃhanāda*; and fifth, *Buddhadhātu*. According to these...

These five names were established based on his deeds. Although *samādhi* (equipoise) applies to all stages, it indicates that Maitreya resides in the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) and is about to achieve perfect awakening; therefore, it is called *Śūraṅgama*.
Regarding the passage from "At that time, the humans and devas... to "...those who made offerings to the śarīra," the commentary states:
The seventh is the offering by humans and devas. In the Sanskrit (Brahma) language, it is called *caitya*, which here means "accumulation. Formerly it was called *tupa*;
this means "stūpa," [the former being] a corruption and abbreviation.
Regarding the passage from "At that time, the Tuṣita Heaven... to "...suddenly manifested through transformation," the commentary states:
The second answer concerns the six aspects of being born in that heaven: first, the place of birth; second, the signs of birth;

third, the physical dimensions and adornments; fourth, extraordinary holy transformations; fifth, the marks and signs and their radiance; and sixth, the benefit of preaching the Dharma. This is [the first].
This is the first [point]. As for the "platform of the seven treasures," it is so called because it is adorned with the seven riches; it is, in fact, the Dharma Hall.
As for the "lion throne," it is because within that platform, the position of the Dharma King is supreme, and he has attained fearlessness. Suddenly—
Regarding the phrase "Jāmbūnada-golden" (□□□□至閻浮檀金色):
the commentary states that this refers to the second characteristic of arising (*utpatti-lakṣaṇa*). Upon the lion throne, there is further a lotus flower;

indeed, upon all Buddha-thrones and within the Pure Lands, one always sits upon a lotus flower. This symbolizes being born from the mire of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and excelling above the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
Because it is turbid water. As for those who sit in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), they place the left foot over the right to sit in the "subduing" posture (*vajraparyaṅka*);
they place the right foot over the left to sit in the "auspicious" posture (*bhadraparyaṅka*). Since he is about to preach the Dharma, he manifests the auspicious posture.
His body color is like gold, signifying that he is worthy of being treasured and honored. The *Anantaprabhā-samādhi Sūtra* states: "Maitreya is the color of white silver."
Speaking in terms of their mutual correspondence: its substance is golden in Jambudvīpa, while the light that shines outward is silver.
Therefore, what is perceived on the surface appears as the color of silver. As stated in the *Sarvajñāprabha-ṛṣi-maitracitta-sūtra*:
"Maitreya is golden in hue, yet within the radiance of white silver, he is adorned with gold, like [a white...]"
The Silver Mountain. Here, too, there is the radiance of white silver. The assembly shall be as before.
Its form is sixteen yojanas in length (up to) that which adorns the celestial crown.
The commentary states: Third, the adornment of the body’s dimensions. Regarding the sixteen *yojanas*:

because his virtue is peerlessly high, he is able to transcend the six realms of existence and surpass the ten stages (*bhūmi*). The significance of his marks and signs will be explained below. As for the lifespan, it is shown in accordance with worldly convention;
thus, it exceeds that of the celestial hosts because his true virtue is supreme. As for the *śakrābhilagna-maṇi* (the Indra’s crest-jewel), it refers to—
Regarding the cintāmaṇi and vaiḍūrya jewels that can manifest in various ways: their shape is like an elongated jade scepter (yángguī), and they resemble red lapis lazuli;
some say they are pure white. Alternatively, it may refer to the name of a tree whose flowers are red, and this jewel resembles them, hence its name.
Regarding the phrase "his celestial crown jewel... abiding within the celestial crown," the commentary states:

this is the fourth extraordinary spiritual transformation (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*), which manifests that his mind is always in the company of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions as his companions.
As for the eighteen transformations: first is "trembling," by which, through mastery over meditative concentration (*samādhi*), he is universally able to cause trembling.

Second, "blazing": on his upper body he emits fierce flames of fire, while beneath his lower body he pours forth clear, cold water—or vice versa—such that his entire body is completely illuminated as various kinds of flames issue forth.
Third, pervasive distribution: because it distributes light that fills countless worlds. Fourth, manifestation:

because it manifests various signs according to what is desired. Fifth, transformation: because all material objects with their own specific characteristics can be transformed in accordance with one's resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).
Sixth, coming and going: because one travels to and fro at will through the body without obstruction.
7. Contraction (*saṃkṣepa*): Because of its power to contract all things, such as the King of Snow Mountains (*Himavat*), into the size of a single atom (*paramāṇu*).
8. Expansion (*prathana*): Because of its power to expand a single atom so that it becomes like the King of Snow Mountains. 9. Entering All Images into the Body (*sarvarūpapraveśana*):

Because of its power to draw all forms and images into one's own body, causing the great assembly to know they have entered the body. 10. Going toward Those of the Same Kind (*sabhāgatopasaṃkrānti*): Following... [text continues]
Eleventh, concealment: because wherever he goes, there is nothing that does not accord with those [beings].
Twelfth, manifestation: because before a great assembly, he again causes his own body to become manifest after having concealed it for hundreds of thousands of eons and so forth.
Thirteenth, mastery over actions: because regarding all matters of coming, going, staying, and so forth, throughout the entire realm of sentient beings, he is himself [masterful].
Because it is transformative. Fourteenth, the mastery over the supernatural powers of others:

the supernatural powers of a Tathāgata are universally able to subdue all others who possess supernatural powers, including the powers manifested by bodhisattvas in their final birth or those possessed by beings in their last existence;
with the exception of the Tathāgatas, they can subdue all others who possess supernatural powers. All other [powers] possessed by those with supernatural powers...
15. Because it is manifest, it can bestow eloquence (*pratibhāna*); for it can grant eloquence that exhausts all [limitations].
16. It can bestow mindfulness (*smṛti*); for if sentient beings have lost their mindfulness regarding the Dharma, it can grant them mindfulness. 17. It can bestow peace and happiness (*sukha*);
for when the True Dharma is taught, it provides the bliss of physical and mental pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) to those who listen to the Dharma.
Eighteenth, he emits great rays of light; his body radiates light throughout countless worlds to cause all sentient beings to pacify their manifold sufferings.
By means of this supernormal power (*abhijñā*), he is able to transform other things that possess an inherent nature (*svabhāva*) into different things;

therefore, it is called "the power of transformation" (*pariṇāmikī ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna-abhijñā*). This is explained in detail in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, in the chapter on "Power" (*Prabhāva-varga*).

Some sutras state that he "dwells within the celestial window," which is a name for the center of the forehead. Although there are two versions of this text, the former follows the *Za* (Miscellaneous) tradition.
It is one *xun* in length; when released, it curls to the right like a conch shell. The commentary explains that this refers to the *ūrṇā-kośa* (tuft of hair) between the eyebrows of all Buddhas.

The space between [the eyebrows] is extremely majestic; thus, the face is the most honored part. The upper space represents the two [eyes], manifesting that the Buddha always values abiding in the Middle Way.
When his noble marks are extended, they are immeasurably long; when retracted, they are like the autumn moon—perfectly bright and radiating light.

White like snow or jade, its radiance illuminates all scenes. White is the fundamental color; it manifests as emotion. It rolls up and unfurls according to the time; it appears in accordance with conditions.
That which flows forth as manifold lights is the most supreme among the characteristics manifested by the shadows of the five vehicles;
therefore, it is specifically described. Regarding the thirty-two marks: beginning from the World-Honored One’s feet, there is the mark of being level and full, wondrously excellent.
It is firm, like the bottom of a casket. Although the ground may be uneven, wherever the feet tread, it is entirely level;
there is no spot that does not touch [the feet] equally, until reaching the crown of the World-Honored One’s head. The *uṣṇīṣa* is lofty, prominent, and perfectly round, like a celestial canopy.
Its breadth is as described in the three hundred and eighty-first fascicle of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, where it is said that the marks of the two [feet] are all produced by a hundred merits.
Therefore, it is said that there are the colors of a hundred jewels and the thirty-two marks. These are the merits induced by practicing five kinds of cultivation:

first, the initial resolve; second, over a long period of time; third, without interruption; fourth, with earnestness; and fifth, without remainder. Consequently, there are five hundred billion colors.
As for the secondary marks (anuvyañjana), there are eighty of them.
They begin with the Blessed One’s fingernails, which are narrow, long, thin, smooth, lustrous, and pure like a flower or red copper;

and they end with the Blessed One’s hands, feet, and chest, all of which possess the auspicious and joyful svastika mark, its patterns like fine embroidery and its color like vermilion, as red as a great... [the sun].

The Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras state that there are five hundred billion such examples, which can be understood through their common characteristics. "Yan" (艶) carries the meaning of beauty, not the meaning of flame.
"Yun" (雲) carries the meaning of producing and providing shade or protection. This arises from practicing eighty-four thousand modes of teaching and conduct.

It counteracts eighty-four thousand types of diseases of the faculties and thereby brings about the primary marks and secondary signs. Consequently, eighty-four thousand colors and lights are emitted.
Master Ji says that the eighty minor marks are brought about by the influence of practicing eighty-four thousand modes of teaching and conduct.
Second, regarding "excellent and beautiful": it states that eighty-four thousand clouds of light emerge. This is likely incorrect;
for the thirty-two marks also arise from eighty-four thousand practices, and it would also contradict the sutra which speaks of two types: marks and excellences (*lakṣaṇānuvyañjana*).
Regarding the passage from "Together with the devaputras" to "the practice of the wheel of Dharma," the commentary states:
There are three aspects to the benefits of the sixth teaching. First, the subject matter is presented; second, the benefits are revealed;
and third, the constant practice is shown. This is the first [of these]. It indicates that the assembly of bodhisattvas has all emerged from the mire of birth and death; therefore, it says:
Each sat upon a lotus throne. Day and night, three times each, constitute what are called the six periods.

Abiding thus during these six periods, they constantly manifest six supernatural transformations (*ṛddhipāda*), preach the practice of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), rescue beings from the six realms of existence (*ṣadgati*), destroy the six underlying tendencies (*ṣadanuśaya*), and give rise to the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).

Some say that this refers to the non-retrogressive practice from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward; others say it refers to the six *pāramitās* practiced by bodhisattvas from the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) upward.
Neither of these views is correct, for all practitioners of the three vehicles—whether ordinary beings or sages—attain their own benefit upon hearing this.
Regarding the phrase "in this very moment attaining *samyak-saṃbodhi*," the commentary states:

"This refers to the benefit of this present life: the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) are produced, the five powers (*pañcabala*) are perfected, and the five eyes (*pañcacakṣus*) shall be brought to fulfillment."
Because they have transcended the five realms of existence, they become five hundred billion devas.
Thus, regarding the description from "In Tuṣita Heaven" up to "the various sons of heaven," it is stated:
"This is their constant activity thereafter. There, it is perpetually bright; there is absolutely no dark night, for the appearance of sleep does not arise."
They obtain the names for night based on this; the Buddha, however, does not do so. He constantly delivers [sermons to] the devaputras.

As for the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* stating that day and night are established according to the blooming and closing of flowers and the singing and silence of birds, this speaks merely of one aspect; in meaning, it is likewise not in contradiction.
Regarding the statement in the *Jāmbūdvīpa-utsaṅga-janma-sūtra*:
the commentary states that this refers to the lifespan of the third dwelling heaven. "Jambū" (in Sanskrit) is the name of a tree;
"Jambudvīpa" (閻浮提) is a corruption of that term. Four hundred years here [on earth] correspond to one day and night in that heaven; thirty such days constitute a month.
Thirty days constitute one month; twelve months constitute one year. The lifespan of those devas is four thousand such years.

Maitreya will descend to be born when he has exhausted that full lifespan, for he does not die prematurely. This scripture states that this corresponds to five hundred and sixty million years in Jambudvīpa.
This is calculated according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Chapter 4), the *Lokaprajñapti-śāstra* (Chapter 7), the *Vibhāṣā*, and other treatises.
Four hundred years [of humans] constitute one day for those [gods].

These four thousand [human years] correspond to one thousand four hundred and forty billion years [for them]. Four thousand years for those gods corresponds to five thousand seven hundred and sixty billion years [for humans].
This contradicts the scriptural text. Now, let us infer by means of reason. First, regarding humans...

Four hundred years [of the human realm] constitute one day and night for them. If one subsequently counts by taking a hundred as a single unit, the calculation will correspond, because one [unit] equals a hundred.
Thus, four thousand years of the human realm constitute ten days for them; four hundred years of the human realm constitute one day for them;
and one thousand four hundred and forty years of the human realm constitute one year for them. Humans...
One thousand four hundred and forty years in that [realm] constitutes one year for them; fourteen million four hundred thousand years in the human world constitutes one hundred years for them;
one billion four hundred and forty million years in the human world constitutes one thousand years for them.
Four thousand years in that [realm] corresponds to five billion seven hundred and sixty million years in the human world. In the western direction, there are three billion such numbers.
One hundred thousand is a *koṭi*; two million is a *koṭi*; three million is a *koṭi*.
By logical inference, taking ten million as one *koṭi* makes the calculation correspond exactly. Therefore, regarding the characters in the sutra:
One should add seven characters. Those first six characters should be placed above "ten thousand" (wan).

This is done only for fear that there may be discrepancies in the recitation of the Sanskrit original, or that the translators may have made errors in their calculations. Otherwise, it would fall short by one hundred and fifty million years;

the principle dictates that it must be so. The wise should understand this. Furthermore, regarding these numerical figures, there are four different versions, according to the *Xiánjié dìngyì* (The Meditative Intent of the Bhadrakalpa).
The Sūtra states: "In five hundred and seventy-six million years, Maitreya shall become a Buddha. Regarding these "five hundred million," it means five billion;
previously, ten million was counted as one "million" (koṭi), thus forming five billion, whereas here, ten thousand times ten thousand is counted as one [unit].
Regarding "one hundred million" (*koṭi*): seventy thousand refers to seven hundred million, because ten thousand constitutes one hundred million. Sixty thousand follows the same numerical principle;
there is no need for further explanation. Although this single scripture differs in its increments and decrements, it accords with the calculations of the treatise.
All other accounts differ. The *Dvaya-parivarta Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that it is one hundred and forty million years;
this does not correspond with this present scripture. Furthermore, the *Sarvajñajyotis-ṛṣi-maitracitta Sūtra* states that it is five hundred and sixty billion years.
The meaning of attaining the Way of the Buddha beneath the Nāgapuṣpa tree has already been explained as before.

Regarding the *Bodhisattva-tsa-t'ai ching* (Sutra on the Bodhisattva’s Dwelling in the Womb) and the *Hsien-yü ching* (Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish), they state: "567,000 years. The six characters [for the number] should actually read seven.
The "seven characters" should be read as "six. As for the "ten million," one hundred is taken as one *koṭi* (one hundred million);

thus, six thousand million is six thousand *koṭis*. This interpretation does not contradict the meaning. Investigating in this manner, although it may differ from ancient commentaries, when one examines the text and investigates the underlying principle, there should be no error.
Regarding the lifespan of a Bodhisattva while in heaven, there has never been any premature death. Born in...
Regarding human life, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states that it lasts for sixty trillion years; when the celestial lifespan is exhausted, the human lifespan is likewise at its peak.

This is because it is appropriate to manifest [the Buddha] during such times. This differs from the case of Śākyamuni, whose celestial lifespan was exhausted while his human life had not yet ended, as sentient beings were weary of suffering and his work of transformation (*saṃdarśana*) was complete.
The *Caturdharmaka-sūtra* (or *Garbhāvakrānti-sūtra*) says that in the human realm, Maitreya’s lifespan will be eighty-four thousand years.

Regarding the "year" (歲): if one relies on the literal text, there is no way to reconcile this. As for Maitreya’s descent to become a Buddha and his benefiting of beings, it is as described in the *Sūtra on the Descent [of Maitreya]* (*Xiasheng jing*).
Once his benefit to the celestial realm is completed, the human capacity for awakening will subsequently ripen; therefore, he descends. Master Ji offers this interpretation.

Although he offers this interpretation, it contradicts the sūtras and śāstras. The teachings of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna state that fifty years among humans [equal one day and night] for the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājika*).
One day and night for [the gods of] the Heaven of the Four Great Kings is equal to five hundred years as the lifespan of those gods.
One day and night for the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven is equal to one thousand years as the lifespan of those gods. Two hundred years in the human realm is one day and night for the Yāma Heaven;

Light. Because it is accomplished through all manner of meritorious virtues, as stated in the thirty-seventh fascicle of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*:

When the merits of each and every such pore are gathered and perfected, they achieve one mark of the Tathāgata.
In this manner, from each individual mark up to the thirty marks, when gathered together, they constitute one hundred [merits].
With twice the merit, one first accomplishes the *ūrṇā-kośa* (the tuft of hair between the eyebrows) of a Tathāgata.

Continuing to cultivate and accumulate [merit], with twice that merit, one accomplishes the *uṣṇīṣa* (the invisible crown protuberance) of a Tathāgata through hundreds of thousands of merits. Question:
Since the light of the *ūrṇā* possesses such merit, why does it only eliminate the sins of ninety billion *kalpas*? Answer: In truth, it does eliminate sins; however, this depends on the individual.

Regarding such sentient beings (up to) "meeting Maitreya," the commentary states:
The sixth section, the summary, establishes the preceding [points] and has four parts: first, attaining birth above; second, descending to be born accordingly;

Having cultivated this, one is later reborn in that heaven; what is there to marvel at? By practicing these six matters of the Dharma, purifying the three karmas to a small degree, and maintaining a single-minded resolve without duality, one will certainly be reborn in the higher realms hereafter.
"He shall also follow Maitreya [until] becoming the very first to hear the Dharma.

"And as for hearing the Dharma":
regarding the phrase "in future ages... until all Buddhas," the commentary states:

Because there will still be other virtuous ones, he shall also encounter the Buddhas of the future eon.

Although the name "Adorned by the Constellations" (*Tārakā-vyūha*) has not been seen in the sacred teachings, its meaning corresponds to the *Bhadrakalpa*; thus, this interpretation is not contradictory.

In those two eons, the thousand Buddhas have already adorned [the world] and will likewise arise according to the constellations; therefore, it is so named. Herein, the three eons are briefly praised.
This is divided into four sections: first, the intent of the establishment; second, the time of the Buddha’s appearance; third, the sequence of the three kalpas;
and fourth, the return to the explanation of the original text. Regarding the first, the intent of the establishment: [the author] asks, for what purpose are these three kalpas established?
Answer: The *Sūtra on the Contemplation of the Bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata* states: "At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha addressed the great assembly, saying:
'In the past, during the period of the final dharma of Tathāgata Prabhāsaśrī, I left the household life to study the Way.
Upon hearing the names of these fifty-three Buddhas, my heart was filled with joy, and I further taught others. Having heard them, those others in turn [taught others...]"
They instructed one another, and even as many as three thousand people, with one voice and in unison, invoked the names of past Buddhas and paid homage with a profound heart.
They immediately attained the transcendence of the sins of birth and death for countless billions of kalpas.
As for those thousand people, they ranged from the Buddha Padmaprabha at the head down to the Buddha Viśvabhū; during the past Adornment Kalpa, they all attained Buddhahood. This...
Regarding the middle thousand Buddhas: beginning with Krakucchanda Buddha and extending down to Ruci Tathāgata, these shall attain Buddhahood within the Bhadrakalpa (Auspicious Aeon).

Regarding the subsequent thousand Buddhas: beginning with Sūryaprabha Tathāgata and extending down to Merudhvaja Buddha, these shall become Buddhas in the future Nakṣatra Kalpa (Constellation Aeon). The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, fascicle six, states: "Beyond..."
The Universal Monarch who preceded [the Buddha] was named Ratnacchattra. The present Tathāgata Ratnārcis was the son of that Universal Monarch’s thousand sons;

the son of the thousand sons of the present Universal Monarch Candraśīrṣa is the present Śākyamuni. According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there were a thousand kalpas in the past during which no Buddhas appeared.
In this single kalpa, however, one thousand Buddhas arise, bringing joy to the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens.

Therefore, they are called the Śuddhāvāsa (Pure Abode) devas. How is this known? When this kalpa is due to have a thousand Buddhas, once the preceding kalpa has ended and everything has become utterly void, a great flood shall arise.
From the bottom of the water, a thousand stalks of seven-jeweled lotuses with radiant light will surge forth;
these are the signs of the thousand Buddhas. The devas of the Pure Abodes know that there are Buddhas because of this. Thus it is said.

This is established based on the causal conditions for three thousand people to resolve their minds toward enlightenment; thus, the three *kalpas* are designated. However, it is not necessarily the case that these three [thousand Buddhas] exist within every single cycle.

Regarding the second question—when a Buddha appears during these three *kalpas*, since there are already one thousand Buddhas therein, do these one thousand Buddhas appear within a single period of formation and destruction (*saṃvarta-vivarta*), or do they span many such periods of formation and destruction?
The Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha replied: [The answer is as follows:]... (The text continues with the response from Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha).
It is said: During the kalpas of formation, destruction, and emptiness, no Buddhas appear; it is only during the kalpa of abiding that Buddhas appear in the world.

Within the twenty kalpas [of the abiding kalpa], Buddhas appear during the first ten kalpas, but not during the latter ten. Even within the former ten kalpas, they do not appear during the first five.
It is in the sixth kalpa that Krakucchanda Buddha appears in the world; in the seventh...
In the [seventh] kalpa, Krakucchanda Buddha appeared; in the eighth kalpa, Kāśyapa Buddha appeared; in the ninth kalpa, Śākyamuni Buddha appeared;
and in the tenth kalpa, Maitreya Buddha will appear. After Maitreya, for immeasurable kalpas, no Buddhas will appear.
Thus we know that one thousand Buddhas cannot all appear within a single kalpa of formation and destruction. Furthermore,

If it is said that there are one thousand Buddhas in the Bhadrakalpa, and that they all reside within a single kalpa of formation and destruction, then since there were also one thousand Buddhas in the past *Vibhūṣaṇakalpa*, they too should have resided within a single kalpa of formation and destruction. If you say they were the same, how so?
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "Just as in that past *Vibhūṣaṇakalpa*, there were the last three Buddhas: Vipaśyin..."
The Buddha [appeared] during the first of the ninety-one kalpas, just as Śikhin Buddha and Viśvabhū Buddha appeared during the thirty-first kalpa.
After that, there were no Buddhas until the ninety-first kalpa, which is the beginning of the Bhadrakalpa (Auspicious Kalpa).
At its start, Krakucchanda Buddha appeared in the world. Having thus spoken of the [Buddha’s] adornments...

The thousand Buddhas of the Bhadra Kalpa appear at different times throughout the preceding and succeeding periods of ninety kalpas, with the final three Buddhas appearing at the end of the Great Kalpa.
From this, we know that the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadra Kalpa likewise do not all appear within a single kalpa of formation and destruction. Master Xuanzang said: [as cited above].
It increases to eighty billion. The *Bhadra-kalpika-sūtra* likewise describes the increase and decrease within a single kalpa. However, the *Lokasthiti-abhidharma-sūtra* states:
"Regarding the period already established and abiding, how much has passed and how much remains? Eight minor kalpas have already passed."
Of the eleven minor kalpas yet to come, the ninth single kalpa has not yet ended in the present.
Within this ninth single kalpa, how much has already passed and how much remains? If it is certain that six hundred and ninety years remain in the future, [then the calculation follows].
There is no contradiction with the Mahāyāna, for this is precisely the position of the Hīnayāna school. Question:
How is it known that within the Mahāyāna school, after the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, there are no further hundred kalpas spent cultivating the karma for the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*)?
Answer: The first chapter of the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra* states: "In the past, at the presence of the Buddha Ratnakoṭi, I fulfilled the first *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*. I kindled..."
Under the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, he fulfilled the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa; under the Buddha Kāśyapa, he fulfilled the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa.
If there were yet another hundred kalpas after these three kalpas, Śākyamuni would not have succeeded Kāśyapa Buddha.
Therefore, we know that for a Mahāyāna bodhisattva practicing the causes, it takes only three kalpas, with no separate hundred kalpas.
There is an interpretation that the two systems are mutually compatible; the texts cited by each are not incorrect, for they represent two doors through which reality is approached.

The first *Vyūha-kalpa* (Adornment Kalpa) must necessarily have been immediately followed by the *Bhadrakalpa* (Auspicious Kalpa).

Therefore, the *Yaoshang jing* (Medicine King Sutra) states that among the thousand Buddhas of the *Vyūha-kalpa*, the one who attained Buddhahood first was named Heguang (Harasvabhāva), and the one who attained Buddhahood last was named Pisheshan (Viśvabhū).
This Viśvabhū is precisely the Buddha of the thirty-first kalpa within the preceding ninety kalpas. This is because after this kalpa...

thus, one knows that the preceding ninety eons were designated as the *Vibhūṣaṇakalpa* (Adornment Eon). As for the *Tārakakalpa* (Constellation Eon), the holy teachings do not provide a fixed enumeration.
The ninth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: The Buddha addressed Ānanda, saying, "These immeasurable bhikṣus who have risen from their seats, from this point forward..."
In the sixty-first kalpa, the Nakṣatra-kalpa (Star Kalpa), they shall all attain Buddhahood, bearing the same title: Mahādhvaja-lakṣaṇa Tathāgata.
By this it may be known that the sixty-first kalpa is the Nakṣatra-kalpa, and all kalpas prior to the Nakṣatra-kalpa are named Bhadrakalpa (the Auspicious Kalpa).
The *Bhadrakalpika-sūtra*, fascicle ten, states: "At that time, the Universal-Wide-Mind Cakravartin King immediately..."
Dīpaṃkara Tathāgata was he. The Buddha’s attendant, named Anihatajñāna, was the bhikṣu Vipaśyin.
The king’s thousand sons are the thousand Buddhas of this Bhadrakalpa. After these thousand Buddhas have passed, for sixty-five kalpas there shall be no Buddhas;
thereafter comes a kalpa called Mahāyaśas, which is identical to this present kalpa.
They attained perfect enlightenment. At that time, eighty thousand ministers, during the eon named Great Renown (*Mahāyaśas*), had already passed away after attaining the path of awakening.

Subsequently, there was an eon named *Tārakopama* (Star-like); within this eon, those eighty thousand ministers attained perfect enlightenment.
After the Constellation Kalpa (*Nakṣatra-kalpa*), the realm will be severed for three hundred intermediate kalpas (*antara-kalpa*) during which no Buddha shall arise.

During that kalpa, eighty-four thousand ladies-in-waiting of this Cakravartin King shall attain perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Judging by this, after the Bhadrakalpa (Auspicious Kalpa), there will be a kalpa of Great Renown (*Mahāyaśas-kalpa*).

"From this point forward, after sixty-one kalpas, during the *Kalpa of Constellations*, you shall attain Buddhahood. Therefore, we know that the *Kalpa of Great Renown* is indeed the *Kalpa of Constellations*. This is the latter interpretation.

The duration of a *kalpa* is not fixed. Regarding the "Constellation Kalpa" (*tārakā-kalpa*), because it encompasses many kalpas in total, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states that the beginning of the Constellation Kalpa is itself named the "Constellation Kalpa," and thus speaks of sixty-one kalpas as constituting the Constellation Kalpa.

There are three types of binding elephants. According to the *Abhidharma*, which relies on the majority of cases, it speaks of three types of *nirvāṇa*; this intention encompasses those such as "grasping the measure.

In the *Abhidharma*, *paiśunya* (slander) is the same as *dvivacana* (divisive speech); though the names differ, the meaning is identical. [End of] *Miśraka*.
The minor school (*hīnayāna*) asserts that only those [actions] which are grave are termed "non-restraint" (*asaṃvara*); others are excluded because they are light.

however, this is incorrect, for it would follow that neutral evil (*madhyama-pāpa*) would also constitute non-restraint. Let us set aside this digression for now.

To explain the text further: those who fall into false views or improper conduct exist everywhere—whether there is a Buddha or not, whether it is central or peripheral—and are found in all directions.

However, if they hear the name of Maitreya, they will certainly not fall [into such states]. This is because their three karmas take refuge [in the Triple Gem], their deep mind is filled with joy, and the power and majesty of their fourfold past vows are added to them.
"Constantly maintaining right view (up to) not slandering the Triple Gem.

this is the opposite of the aforementioned falling into dark places or being born in borderlands, for such a person constantly encounters the Triple Gem and gives rise to faith and inclination.

Not only is there an absence of middle-grade evil, but there is also the arising of upper and lower grades of the three kinds of goodness, which are established according to their respective conditions. This is intended to clarify that even upon merely hearing the name...
