The commentary states: The third section distinguishes rebirth in the lower grade. This refers to those who have committed various transgressions of the precepts but attain rebirth through purification by repentance.
Within this, there are three parts: first, the extinction of offenses through repentance and the practice leading to rebirth; second, seeing the sages and attaining non-retrogression;

and third, encountering future Buddhas. The first part further has three sub-sections: first, the extinction of offenses; second, the practice; and third, rebirth. This is the first: the extinction of offenses.
There are two types: first, those who previously received the precepts but later violated them;

second, those who previously did not receive the precepts and committed various evil deeds, yet upon hearing the name [of the Buddha], they take refuge and pay homage by prostrating with their two hands, two feet, and head—casting down their five limbs to the ground.
Through sincere repentance, one's offenses are swiftly purified.
Regarding those who, in future ages, shall perform prostrations and maintain mindfulness, it is said:
"This is the practice of cultivation. Even if one has not committed offenses, if one repents and vows to be reborn [in the Pure Land], one need only cultivate the ten practices."
One will certainly be reborn there by means of these ten [practices]: first, hearing his name; second, fashioning images; third, offering incense; fourth, offering flowers; fifth, offering robes;
sixth, offering silk canopies; seventh, offering banners; eighth, offering pennants; ninth, constantly prostrating with the body;
and tenth, constantly binding the mind in mindfulness.
Regarding the passage "when this person’s life ends... they shall attain rebirth," the commentary states:
"This refers to rebirth hereafter. Even those who have violated the precepts or committed evil deeds may attain rebirth by taking refuge in purity, hearing the Name, and practicing accordingly."
When his life was about to end, the Bodhisattva emitted the wondrous light from the white tuft between his brows, which extinguished the darkness of his transgressions.

He rained down the exquisite colors of variegated flowers, causing the seeds of the Path to grow. Buddhas and devas came to welcome him, manifesting the depth of their compassion; thus, in an instant, he attained rebirth in the Pure Land.
This is because it manifests the excellence of their karma. While this is the general characteristic, to explain in detail:
those who repent, fashion images, make offerings, prostrate, and maintain constant mindfulness will be born in the upper grade of the lower level.

Those who repent, fashion images, and make offerings, yet do not constantly prostrate or maintain mindfulness, will be born in the middle grade of the lower level. Those who repent and fashion images, and merely make offerings, but do not constantly prostrate... [text ends].

Regarding those who constantly maintain mindfulness: even for those of the lowest-of-the-low grade who are reborn there, although they have repented their sins and attained their eradication, they may not have fashioned images, nor performed offerings and prostrations;
or perhaps they have only fashioned images, or only made offerings, or only prostrated, or only maintained focused mindfulness, or merely recited the name once—this is the lowest-of-the-low grade.
Even if they are not reborn there, they will nonetheless attain [liberation] within the three assemblies.
"Delivered and liberated.
Regarding those who encounter Maitreya and attain non-retrogression, the commentary states:
"Second, seeing the Sage and not retreating. Their roots of goodness have long been matured; upon seeing him, they immediately pay homage. Compassion arises of its own accord..."

They arise; they quickly hear the Dharma; they eliminate lack of faith; and they swiftly attain non-retrogression. Some say that within the stage of the ten levels of faith, the mind of non-retrogression is called "attaining non-retrogression."
Regarding the phrase "in future ages... [until] attaining all Buddhas and Tathāgatas," the commentary states:

this refers to the third stage of encountering Buddhas. That is to say, in the future, one will encounter the Buddhas of the *Tārakā-kalpa* (Star Constellation Eon) following the sands of Ganges rivers;
it does not refer to the Buddhas within the *Tārakā-kalpa* itself. Were it otherwise, it would contradict the three lifetimes mentioned in the superior grade.
It is solely because they encounter the Buddhas of the *tārakā-kalpa* that they are reborn in these higher realms.
Although they are born in three categories and nine grades, they all belong to the inner assembly, where they personally behold the Buddha and swiftly hear the Dharma.

If they are born among the outer assembly, even those of the ninth grade will spontaneously attain the stage of non-retrogression at a later time; the name of the Buddha will be Maitreya, for their roots of goodness have naturally matured. This...
The account of the initial cultivation of practice and rebirth is hereby concluded.
The Buddha told Upāli [up to] "becoming one who provides great refuge.
The commentary states: Second, the general exhortation to take refuge in the Noble Ones for the attainment of wholesome benefits has three parts. First, the Noble Ones act as the refuge.
Next is taking refuge, which means non-retrogression; later, one will see the light and receive a prediction of enlightenment. This is the first [of these].
After Śākyamuni’s parinirvāṇa, sentient beings of the five realms of existence will sink into the ocean of suffering, having nothing to rely upon.

Since they have not yet encountered a Buddha of true recompense, they all belong to the Compassionate Honored One (Maitreya), who acts as their refuge to bring them across. If they do not see him, they will lose this great benefit; therefore, it is called the "Great Refuge."
Regarding the locus:

it is said that if one takes refuge [and so forth] until attaining non-retrogression, this indicates that by taking refuge in this way, one attains non-retrogression. Some say that by taking refuge in Maitreya, one immediately enters the stage [of certainty].
This is not so. Entering the stage means entering the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).

Although one has practiced for many kalpas, it is now explained that by encountering Maitreya, one will certainly attain Bodhi and reach the state of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*), as this is taught regarding the stage of faith.
Regarding the passage from "Maitreya Bodhisattva" up to "immediately received the prediction," the commentary states:
"This refers to the subsequent reception of the prediction. *Tathāgata* means "Thus Come One. *Arhat*.
It is so. The Triple [Body] of the Buddha is the Perfectly Complete Enlightened One (*samyaksaṃbuddha*). Those who have attained the holy ones behold him with the light of wisdom;
whereas ordinary persons see him with their eyes as golden in color. Since the cause does not regress, the fruit is likewise unsurpassed.

The third section shows the amount of sin extinguished by those who have taken refuge in the Noble Ones. There are three categories and nine grades.

For those who vow to be reborn [in the Pure Land], they cultivate the ten virtuous actions, maintain mindfulness of the Name, and pay respectful homage; because the sins extinguished differ accordingly, there are two parts within this, the first of which is the analysis.

One is born when the karma for birth in the realm of bliss is fulfilled. Later, it will be explained that even if one does not practice with joy, the cause remains incomplete. Furthermore, there are four initial stages:
first, causing mindfulness; second, encouraging practice; third, teaching aspiration; and fourth, extinguishing transgressions. This refers to the first.
By means of focused mindfulness and contemplation, taking a virtuous mind as the basis, one establishes the cause for rebirth in Tuṣita Heaven.
Regarding those who desire to be reborn in Tuṣita Heaven (up to) those who practice the ten paths of wholesome action:
the commentary states that this is the second exhortation to practice. For now, it discusses the observance of the precepts and does not speak of other deeds, citing only the very minimum.
Whether it be for one day up to seven days, one will still attain rebirth; how much more so for those who have practiced for many years and many lifetimes with every kind of goodness?

Since all virtues are subsumed within the ten wholesome actions (*daśa-kuśala-karmapatha*), one should contemplate them. As for the practice, that which is most weighty is called the Path of the Ten Wholesome Actions.
Some say that specific prior practices are the cause for rebirth, while others maintain that the ten wholesome actions as a whole are the cause for rebirth; this is not the case.

Regarding the precepts and the paths of action (*karmapatha*), because there are distinctions in their practice and cultivation, it is said that one who possesses these merits should engage in contemplation.

This is described as the third teaching on aspiration (*praṇidhāna*). If there is practice without aspiration, the practice will necessarily be solitary; it will not necessarily lead to rebirth [in the Pure Land].
Because of Maitreya’s intent, there may be aspiration without practice, yet such aspiration will inevitably be empty. Since there was no prior cause, the fruit cannot arise;
therefore, the teaching holds that aspiration and practice must support one another.
Regarding the passage from "One who performs this contemplation" to "the sins of birth and death," the commentary states:
The fourth [section], the elimination of sins, has three parts. First, encountering conditions and fixing the mind; second, hearing the name and giving rise to reverence;

third, prostrating and surrendering with sincerity. This first [part], encountering conditions, has three [aspects]. The first is sentient beings; that is, seeing a celestial being (*deva*). Accordingly...

Upon encountering a single sentient being, one should immediately call to mind Maitreya: if they are suffering, one thinks of uprooting that suffering; if they lack joy, one thinks of bestowing it upon them;

The father of Kāśyapa Buddha was named Brahmadatta, of the Brāhmaṇa caste; his mother was named Dhanavatī.

At that time, the king was named King Kiki, and the kingdom he governed was named Vārāṇasī. Although other names differ, these distinctions arise from the varying conventions of the Chinese and the barbarians.
There should be no contradiction. During the time of Vipaśyin Buddha, there was a minister named Tiṣya; the rest may be verified elsewhere.
This refers to one capable of distinguishing [the boundaries] up to the various realms of a kingdom.
The commentary states: This section praises present wisdom. Since the present world-systems are without measure or number, they cannot be discussed in full detail;
a brief summary is provided as found in the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*.
Furthermore, it is clearly understood [up to] "the Truly Perfectly Awakened One.

The commentary states: This subsequently praises future wisdom. Although this wisdom illuminates the Buddhas of the future, because Maitreya is the one who will guide and transform [beings], Ānanda wishes to inquire;
thus, for the time being, he cites the events of the Śaṅkha era.
Regarding the request to hear about the transformations (up to the question of how long they will last), the narrative states:
this is the second petition, requesting five matters. First, the Buddha’s supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), which refers to the transformation itself.

Second, the number of the assembly, which refers to the disciples who follow as attendants. Third, Maitreya’s attainment of Buddhahood, which refers to the Buddha. Fourth, the reliance... [text fragment].
"Adornment of retribution" refers to the abundance and joy of the environment. "The duration of his dwelling in the world" refers to the length of time spent in the sutra.

Some say that "change" refers to the fact that the lands and their inhabitants are not fixed from beginning to end; thus it is called change, but this does not refer to a transformation by supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), as there is no other answer provided.
Regarding "the duration," this asks about the period of five hundred and sixty million years, rather than the time he actually dwells [in the world].
This is not so. In the first five causes, the Tathāgata sees both the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) and the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) of the Bodhisattva coming to welcome him.

Speaking in terms of predominance, it is solely by cultivating the cause of giving that one attains the vision of the Sage; for through the practice of giving, one is able to relinquish material wealth and establish [images of] the physical form.
The images and various offerings represent the holy ones; thus, one sees the transformation bodies coming to welcome and receive them.

When asked about the two conditions of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), why is it that they are not seen? This is because seeing the holy ones is manifested through the practice of giving.

However, if discussed according to reality, the cultivation of the causes of concentration and wisdom both possess the meaning of beginning with initial practice and ending in accomplishment. If one considers the final stage...
One achieves a meditative concentration that accords with reason and internally realizes true wisdom. One truly sees the Bodhisattva’s emanation coming to welcome one.
Now, based on the initial stage of cultivation, one has not yet accorded with the principle of realization; therefore, one does not see [the Bodhisattva] who has already perfected the practice.

Because the place manifested is superior, it is distinguished by way of this [superiority]. Thus, the difference in the manner of being born above is shown. Fourth, it clarifies the benefits obtained upon birth. Since the causes are numerous, the benefits obtained—

The benefits are indeed manifold; though they are beyond number, based on this sutra, there are two types of benefit: first, the benefit of extinguishing transgressions, and second, the benefit of hearing the Dharma.
Regarding the first benefit, there are six aspects. First is the benefit of taking refuge. As the sutra says:

"Having paid homage, one contemplates the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows with focused attention, and immediately transcends the sins of birth and death for ninety billion kalpas. Second is the benefit of paying homage...

The benefit of paying respect is as stated in the sutra: "If there are those who pay homage to Maitreya Bodhisattva, they shall eliminate the sins of birth and death accumulated over ten billion kalpas.
The benefit of hearing his name three times is as stated in the sutra: "Whoever merely hears this name of Maitreya..."
1. Not falling into the darkness, the borderlands, wrong views, or evil disciplines. 2. Eradicating sins and obtaining benefits. As the sutra says:
"Merely hearing the name of Maitreya and joining one's palms in reverence removes the sins of fifty kalpas of birth and death.
3. Obtaining benefits by hearing the invocation of his name. As the sutra says: "If for even a single moment one invokes the name of Maitreya, this person shall eliminate [their transgressions]."
Regarding the transgressions of birth and death over twelve hundred kalpas, there are six ways to obtain benefit through repentance. As the sutra says:

"If men or women have violated various prohibitions and precepts or committed numerous evil deeds, upon hearing the name of this Bodhisattva of Great Compassion, they prostrate themselves with their five limbs touching the ground and repent with a sincere heart;
these various evil karmas will swiftly become purified. Regarding the subsequent benefits of the Dharma, there are three types.

First, obtaining benefit upon hearing the Dharma. As the sutra says: "At that time, the Bodhisattva, according to their past affinities, expounded the sublime Dharma for them, causing them to strengthen their causal roots and not regress from the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment. Second, obtaining benefit through encountering a sage has three aspects.
First, the benefit of meeting a sage in the present. As the sutra says: "They encountered Maitreya and, following Maitreya, descended to Shan."
Jambudvīpa. First, the benefit of hearing the Dharma; second, the benefit of being born in the presence of a Sage. As the sutra says: "One encounters all the Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa.
Third, the benefit of encountering Sages in the future. As the sutra says: "In the future, one shall encounter Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Regarding the third point, the benefit of receiving a prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*), there are two aspects. First, receiving the prophecy of Bodhi from Maitreya. As the sutra says:
It is said: "If there are those who take refuge in Maitreya Bodhisattva, you should know that such persons shall attain non-retrogression on the path to unsurpassed enlightenment.

When the Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, they shall behold the Buddha’s radiance and immediately receive a prediction of their own enlightenment. Subsequently, they shall receive predictions from all the Buddhas.
As the sutra says: 'During the Constellation Kalpa (Nakṣatra-kalpa), they shall likewise encounter the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones,' and under these Buddhas..."
Previously, the prediction of enlightenment (*bodhi-vyākaraṇa*) was granted; let this digression cease for now, and we shall return to the explanation of the text.

This is the fifth section. Within it, there are three parts: first, the exhortation to perform the practices for rebirth there; second, the assembly’s expression of rarefied aspirations; and third, the conclusion establishing correct contemplation.

Regarding the first part, there are again three sub-sections: first, the cultivation of causes for rebirth, wherein the categories differ; second, the general exhortation to take refuge in the Noble Ones; and third, the realization [of the goal].

Excellent benefit! Next, the return to the Noble Ones is shown. Regarding the extent of the destruction of sins, there are three stages: initial, middle, and final. First is that produced by superior causes;
next is that produced by middling causes; finally is that produced by inferior causes. Within the first stage, there are further six parts. The first demonstrates the cultivation of the cause.

Second, the teaching on the dedication of vows; third, the actual rebirth; fourth, the praise and exhortation of the devas; fifth, the benefits of being born there; sixth, the summary that concludes the above.
Regarding the first [of these six], there are two parts: first, the general expression, which is the diligent cultivation of merit;

second, the specific explanation, which refers to the causes consisting of six matters. What are these six? First, the practice of guarding the precepts, meaning that one's dignified demeanor (*īryāpatha*) is not deficient.

Therefore: (2) The practice of revering the stūpa, which consists of sweeping the stūpa and smearing the ground with plaster; (3) The practice of making offerings, which consists of offering various kinds of famous incense and exquisite flowers;
(4) The practice of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which consists of practicing various *samādhis* and entering into right absorption (*samāpatti*);

(5) The practice of reciting and chanting the sūtras; and (6) The practice of chanting the sūtras, which consists of reading and reciting the scriptures. Some say: (1) The practice of majestic deportment...
The ritual procedures are not deficient.
Second, since the Hīnayāna schools differ from one another, how can the various teachings be standardized into a single system? Now, this explanation is made based on the Hīnayāna school:
it is not necessarily the case that the three *kalpas* arise in immediate succession during a period of decline, because the Buddha’s wholesome qualities are few. Now, based on...
In the Mahāyāna, the three eons must necessarily proceed without interruption because of the abundance of roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
The eons of formation, abiding, and destruction are respectively termed the *Vyuṣita-kalpa*, the *Bhadra-kalpa*, and the *Tārakā-kalpa*; there is no contradiction in this principle.

Let this digression cease for now, and we shall return to the explanation of the text. This is the fourth section. "Bodhi" means awakening, as it is the awakening to all phenomena. "Bestowal" (*pradāna*) is also called...

"Receiving" (*pratigraha*) refers to the disciple; "bestowing" (*vyākaraṇa*) refers to the Tathāgata. Because the Tathāgata bestows [the prophecy] and records that [the disciple] will certainly attain [enlightenment], it is called "bestowing a prophecy" (*vyākaraṇa*).

Because the disciple grasps the meaning and believes that it is not false, it is called "receiving a prophecy" (*pratigraha*). Prior to expounding the bestowal of prophecy, there are briefly five sections:

first, the intent of bestowing prophecy; second, the one who bestows the prophecy; third, the person to whom the prophecy is bestowed; fourth, the distinctions of time; [and fifth, the distinctions of the prophecy itself].
5. Explanation of the Text. First, the Intent of Bestowing Prophecy. When the Tathāgata bestows prophecy, there are five underlying intentions: first, the Great Master’s retroactive illumination;
second, the certainty that a cause must yield its fruit; third, causing others to give rise to reverence; fourth, not abandoning sentient beings, as they possess the potential for Buddhahood;
and fifth, because their stage of practice and rank are already high. For these five reasons, it is necessary to bestow the prophecy of Bodhi.

Furthermore, regarding the second [point], the bestowal of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*): the Buddha has three bodies (*trikāya*). Some say that if he bestows predictions upon those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) or bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), it is exclusively the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
If he bestows predictions upon bodhisattvas of the great stages (*mahābhūmi*), it also includes the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*).

Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "The transformation body preaches the Dharma for the two vehicles and bodhisattvas prior to the stages; the enjoyment body [preaches it] for the [great stages]."
The *Lankavatara Sutra* states that the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha bestows predictions upon the Nirmāṇakāya Śrāvakas, while the Dharmatā-niṣyanda-kāya Buddha bestows distinct predictions.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that the Dharmatā-niṣyanda-kāya Buddha preaches the Dharma, which can be received by Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
This interpretation is incorrect; for if the Nirmāṇakāya transforms for Bodhisattvas of the great earth (*mahābhūmi*), the Saṃbhogakāya likewise...

This is because [the Buddha] manifests as the Two Vehicles and ordinary beings. If this were not admitted, it would contradict the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, which states that through the empowerment of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), they are made to see [the Buddha] for a time.
Although the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) also preaches the Dharma and bestows predictions (*vyākaraṇa*), there is a difference in meaning;

therefore, one must say that those who bestow [predictions] are necessarily the Transformation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the Other-Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*). This can be understood through reflection. Chapter [X].

There are five types of persons who receive the prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*). As stated in the *Sambhāra-śāstra*: first, those who have not yet resolved their minds; second, those who have resolved their minds together [with others];

third, the concealed; fourth, the manifest; and fifth, the intentional (*saṃdhyābhāṣita*). The first four are granted the prophecy for persons of the Mahāyāna, while the last one is granted for persons of the Hīnayāna.

Regarding the first, those who have not yet resolved their minds, some say they correspond to the stage of the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), because they have attained superior faith (*adhimukti*).

Not so. Even those prior to the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) have already resolved their minds toward enlightenment; how much more so those within the ten stages of faith who have not yet done so?

To explain this now: from time immemorial until the point when the bodhicitta has not yet been generated, the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* (Treatise on the Great Vehicle) classifies this as the "Stage of Nature" (*gotrabhūmi*), which is precisely the nature-lineage (*prakṛti-gotra*).
As the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* says: "This person wanders through the five paths..."

Their faculties are sharp and they delight in the Great Dharma. The Buddha knows that after a certain number of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, such persons shall attain the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Regarding those who subsequently resolve their minds together with them, some say this refers to the stages of the ten understandings (*daśa-adhimukti*) and the ten practices (*daśa-carita*), because they have attained superior practice;
however, this is not so, for even those at the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) have already resolved their minds.
Now, it is explained that the desire for wholesome dharmas is called "arousing the mind" (bodhicitta). As that treatise states:

"Maturing the roots of goodness, planting the seed of enlightenment, and attaining superior practices—this is solely because of the desire to liberate all sentient beings. Thus, at the very moment the mind is aroused...

They enter the stage of non-retrogression; they possess no quality of falling back; they are free from the eight unfavorable conditions (the eight *akṣaṇas*). Next, regarding those who conceal [their realization]:

from the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*) down to the seventh stage (*bhūmi*), if they hear their own prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), they do not arouse diligence toward the practice of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*);
yet if they do not hear it, they do arouse it. This is intended to sever the distracting thoughts of others. How long must such a bodhisattva exert themselves with diligent effort?

Because they have attained certainty regarding *bodhi*, they are granted the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). Some say that up until the seventh stage (*bhūmi*), one has not yet attained [the state where] there is no falling back by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*), because there is still occasional falling back from practice.
This is not so; for once one has practiced from the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) onward, one will certainly not fall back. Next, as for those who appear before [the Buddha]:

if a bodhisattva achieves the five supramundane faculties (*indriya*), attains the patience toward the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and dwells in the Immovable Stage (*acalā bhūmi*).
Time has no before or after, for all Buddhas appear before one and bestow the prophecy of attaining Buddhahood.
Regarding the later "intentional meaning" (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*), as stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*: "We all rejoice; such is the intentional speech of the Great Sage."
